frases.texto: Berkshire Hathaway, a legendary stock, fell twenty percent in 1999 while the market soared.
If you owned it, Warren Buffett looked finished.
Selling right there is the most common mistake in investing.
The next year, the tech bubble burst.
Berkshire went up while the market went down.
That wasn't even its worst year.
Years earlier, it had crashed even harder.
The people who held from the start earned almost twenty percent a year.
The market earned about ten.
But for every Berkshire, thousands of stocks fell and never came back.
This is not advice.
Remember Berkshire in 1999 the next time the market scares you.
Berkshire Hathaway, the best stock of the last half century, lost twenty percent in 1999.
Most people who sold that year never got back in.
So why did Buffett refuse to chase tech?
He said he could not understand those businesses.
The next year, the tech bubble burst.
Berkshire went up while the market went down.
Over six decades it compounded almost twenty percent a year.
The market did about ten.
But for every Berkshire, thousands of stocks fell and never came back.
This is not advice.
Remember Berkshire the next time a bad year scares you.

ganchos.texto: Berkshire Hathaway, a legendary stock, fell twenty percent in 1999 while the market soared.
Berkshire Hathaway, a legendary stock, trailed the market by forty points in 1999.
Berkshire Hathaway, a legendary stock, looked broken in 1999.

error.nota: Story advances at the midpoint (bubble bursts, Berkshire rises) instead of explaining a statistic.

misterio.nota: Buffett quote on tech needs its own source; f2 claim is unverifiable.

error+g1.nota: Clear story start; 'fell twenty percent' is concrete but common.

error+g2.nota: Forty-point gap is hard to believe and verified (-19.9 vs +21.0); opens the why.

error+g3.nota: 'Looked broken' is vague, no number to anchor.
